(8) Low-income buyers of uncertified electric motorcycles or conversion kits — exposed to fire risk in dense housing and to worthless warranties. (9) Owners of failed brands — Neta buyers already, more to follow. (10) Residents of eastern Indonesia generally — bearing the extraction externalities while having the least access to the vehicles, charging and industrial value-added.
kasus_china: (1) BYD — the definitive case. A battery maker that entered cars in 2003, survived on subsidies and buses, chose LFP when the industry chose NMC, vertically integrated from cells to semiconductors, and reached ~4.6 million deliveries with over 1.05 million exports in 2025 and a workforce that peaked above 900,000. It also shows the limits: a reported ~100,000-job cut (~10%) in 2025 as growth slowed and the price war bit. (2) Neta / Hozon New Energy — the counter-case. A mid-tier brand that grew on subsidies and price competition, expanded internationally including into Southeast Asia, then entered bankruptcy restructuring, stranding owners without service and damaging the reputation of Chinese EVs in export markets — the single most relevant cautionary case for Indonesian consumers and regulators, given Neta's presence in Indonesia. (3) The 2016 subsidy-fraud investigation — 93 companies probed, 72 found fraudulent, 76,374 phantom vehicles, RMB 9.27 billion; the case that forced China to redesign subsidies around post-verification and accumulated mileage, and the clearest transferable lesson for Indonesian incentive design. (4) Shenzhen — the fleet-first template: fully electrified bus fleet by 2017 and taxi fleet by 2019 through municipal mandate plus BYD supply, demonstrating that public-fleet electrification creates the volume, charging demand and technician base that private adoption later rides on. (5) Liuzhou and the Wuling Hongguang Mini EV — a sub-USD 5,000 micro-EV plus municipal parking and charging concessions produced mass adoption in a mid-tier industrial city on incomes far below Beijing's; the most directly transferable model for Indonesian secondary cities and the one Indonesia has conspicuously not copied. (6) The licence-plate quota exemption in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen — academic evaluation using synthetic control finds the free-plate effect exceeded the purchase-subsidy effect, making it the highest-return, lowest-cost instrument China deployed. (7) CATL — from a 2011 startup to the world's largest cell maker, and now the counterparty in Indonesia's USD 6 billion East Halmahera project; the case that defines what Indonesia is trying and failing to replicate domestically. (8) The 2023-2025 price war and anti-involution response — Tesla's January 2023 cuts, 227 models discounting in 2024, margins at 4.3%, 738 → 591 makers, the June 2025 60-day supplier-payment rule; the case showing that a successful transition generates its own destructive dynamics requiring a second round of regulation. (9) The informal battery-recycling grey market — 70-75% of retired packs, ~RMB 10,000 profit per vehicle, documented fires, poisoning and water contamination; the failure Indonesia still has time to avoid. (10) The January 2026 purchase-tax halving — a decade-long, pre-announced taper (RMB 30,000 cap to RMB 15,000, effective 5% rate), the opposite of Indonesia's abrupt subsidy cliff.
padanan_indonesia: (1) BYD Indonesia — entered January 2024, became the best-selling BEV brand with ~39.7% of BEV wholesales by mid-2025 and 51% of full-year 2025 BEV sales including Denza, reached top-six overall car brand, and is building a ~USD 1 billion, 150,000-unit plant at Subang for 2026 production. The closest analogue to the TikTok Shop pattern in e-commerce: direct corporate transplantation producing market leadership within roughly twelve months. (2) Wuling Air ev — the first BEV mass-produced in Indonesia (Cikarang, 2022), a direct descendant of the Liuzhou micro-EV playbook and proof that the Chinese small-EV model can be localised, though it has since lost share to BYD. (3) The CATL/CBL-ANTAM-IBC USD 6 billion integrated project — groundbreaking in East Halmahera on 29 June 2025 with a 6.9 GWh first-phase cell plant in Karawang, projecting 8,000 direct and 35,000 indirect jobs; Indonesia's attempt to convert nickel into battery-chain participation, and the test case for whether downstreaming delivers capability or only extraction. (4) The Rp 7 million electric-motorcycle subsidy (2023-2024) and its aftermath — sales rose to 62,409 (2023) and 77,078 (2024), then fell 28.6% to 55,059 in 2025 when the subsidy lapsed; the sharpest available evidence that Indonesian EV demand is currently policy-manufactured rather than self-sustaining, and the exact opposite of China's decade-long taper. (5) Polytron — an Indonesian consumer-electronics brand that took a claimed ~60% share of a shrinking electric-motorcycle market with roughly 33,000 units, built on Chinese componentry; the closest thing to a domestic champion, and a reminder that 'local' in this domain means localised assembly of Chinese technology. (6) IMIP Morowali — the Indonesian counterpart to China's industrial clusters, but with the costs concentrated locally: 21 deaths in the December 2023 explosion, tailings dam breaches in March 2025, and tailings volumes projected to reach ~47 million tonnes a year. (7) Neta Indonesia — stranded by its parent's bankruptcy, the local instance of China's brand-failure risk. (8) The TKDN escalator (40% 2026, 60% 2027-2028, 80% 2030) — Indonesia's substitute for China's dual-credit mandate: a localisation lever rather than an electrification lever, which is a meaningful design difference. (9) PLN's SPKLU network — 4,655 units at 3,007 locations by end-2025, +44% YoY, roughly China's 2013-2014 position. (10) The RUKN decree cutting the 2030 electric-motorcycle target from 13 million to 2.9-3.8 million — the moment the government formally conceded that the Chinese two-wheeler pattern will not reproduce here.

Rendah (Low) for all forward projections — Indonesian mainstream and peak years, the two-wheeler inflection date, and the durability of the nickel-battery investment thesis — and for the China two-wheeler fleet total, where estimates range from ~300 million to ~380 million depending on source and whether unregistered units are counted.
catatan_kontradiksi_data: (1) The '51% NEV share' in the research brief does not match the CAAM full-year 2025 figure of 47.9%; 51%+ figures refer to monthly retail penetration (CPCA basis, which first crossed 50% in July 2024) or to specific months of 2025. Annual vs monthly and wholesale vs retail are routinely conflated in secondary reporting. (2) The claim that Indonesia's top-10 EV brands are 'all Chinese' is close but not exact: the Jan-May 2025 top ten includes Hyundai (Korean, 3.1%) and Citroën (Stellantis, 0.5%); eight of ten are Chinese-owned brands, and Chinese brands hold roughly 94-96% of BEV volume. (3) The brief's '~0.6-1%' electric-motorcycle share is confirmed (55,059 of ~6.55 million ≈ 0.84% in 2025) but the direction is important and often missed: the share fell in 2025, it did not rise. (4) Indonesian EV population figures vary by source and date — 342,118 (Kemenhub, 2025), ~358,000 (another 2025 count), 386,591 (July 2026) — because of differences between registration, SRUT and police-registry bases. (5) Indonesian electric-motorcycle sales data come variously from AISI and from Kemenhub SRUT and do not always agree; SRUT counts type-tested registrations rather than retail deliveries. (6) BYD's reported 2025 revenue of 'RMB 8.0396 trillion' in one source is implausible by an order of magnitude and was not used here; the delivery figure (~4.6 million, >1.05 million exported) and the ~100,000-job reduction are more consistently reported but the job cut is single-sourced [uncertain]. (7) China's electric two-wheeler fleet is cited as 300+ million, ~380 million (China Bicycle Association) and 400 million depending on source and whether non-compliant/unregistered units are included. (8) 2025 e-two-wheeler production of 63.16 million units against H1 domestic sales of 32.33 million implies a large export and inventory component that sources do not decompose. (9) LG Energy Solution's reported withdrawal in 2025 from the larger 'Grand Package' battery consortium — subsequently taken up by CATL — was referenced in industry commentary but was not verified against a primary source in this research [uncertain]. (10) GIAMM-linked estimates that EV manufacturing absorbs ~500,000 workers versus ~1.5 million in the conventional chain come from industry advocacy and should be treated as directional rather than measured. (11) Nickel-smelter casualty figures (104 accidents, 107 deaths, 155 injuries, 2019-2025) are NGO/journalist compilations; no consolidated official series exists. (12) Indonesia's charging-point totals differ between PLN's own network (4,655 units at 3,007 locations, end-2025) and 'national' figures near 5,000 that include private operators; the March 2025 figure of 3,772 SPKLU cited by ESDM is an earlier point in the same series, not a contradiction. (13) The 2030 electric-motorcycle target exists in two official versions — 13 million (Perpres-linked roadmap) and 2.9-3.8 million (Kepmen ESDM 85.K/2025 RUKN) — and government communications still cite both.
